title: FreRA: A Frequency-Refined Augmentation for Contrastive Learning on Time Series Classification

problem.claim: Optimal augmentation design is important for contrastive learning on time series classification tasks.

gap.claim: Existing predefined time-domain augmentations are mainly adopted from vision and may introduce mismatched patterns that distort semantically relevant time-series information.

contributions.claim: FreRA is a lightweight frequency-refined augmentation tailored for time-series contrastive learning and designed for plug-and-play integration with contrastive learning frameworks.
FreRA separates critical and unimportant frequency components and applies semantic-aware identity modification to the former and semantic-agnostic self-adaptive modification to the latter.
The authors prove that FreRA generates semantic-preserving views.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly present a novel frequency-domain perspective for designing augmentations for time-series contrastive learning.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive experiments on two benchmark archives, UCR and UEA, and five large-scale datasets from diverse applications.
The authors report that FreRA consistently outperforms ten leading baselines on time-series classification, anomaly detection, and transfer learning tasks.
The authors report superior contrastive representation learning and transfer-learning generalization across diverse datasets.

narrative_sequence.summary: Contrastive learning is presented as an effective approach for unsupervised representation learning.
Optimal augmentation strategies for time-series classification are underexplored, and vision-derived time-domain augmentations may be incompatible with time-series semantics.
The frequency domain is motivated by global feature encoding, orthogonal component isolation, and preservation of semantic integrity with a compact component set.
FreRA separates critical and unimportant frequency components and modifies them differently to protect relevant information while adding variance.
The authors report a theoretical semantic-preservation result and empirical improvements across benchmark and large-scale datasets and multiple tasks.

source_observation.claim: The method distinguishes critical from unimportant frequency components and applies different modification policies to them.

interpretation.claim: Augmentation may be safer when it protects components associated with semantic information while concentrating variability in less important components.

application.claim: For time-series contrastive learning, frequency-aware augmentation can be considered as a plug-and-play alternative to generic vision-derived time-domain transformations.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this strategy transfers to datasets, tasks, or conditions beyond those reported.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the component-separation criterion or modification algorithms.
The abstract does not provide dataset sizes, quantitative results, or experimental settings.
